Description: explicit — client-side hypsometric tint (color-relief layer, GL JS 5.6+)
prompt: I have terrain tiles as a raster-dem source in MapLibre GL JS and I want to color the map by elevation ranges (a hypsometric tint) directly client-side — blues at sea level through greens and browns to white peaks — without pre-rendering colored raster tiles. What layer type do I use and how do I configure the color ramp?

Provide steps, maybe also mention that no raster layer, no raster-color. Provide notes about opacity, resampling, etc. Provide full code snippet. Also mention that you can adjust exaggeration, etc. Provide final answer. **Short answer** *Use a **`color‑relief`** layer.* It reads the same `raster-dem` source that you already have and lets you tint the terrain on‑the‑fly with an **`interpolate`** expression over the special `["elevation"]` expression. Below is a complete, copy‑and‑paste‑ready example that shows: 1. Adding the DEM source (if you haven’t already). 2. Adding a `color‑relief` layer that paints the DEM with a hypsometric ramp (blue → green → brown → white). 3. Optional tweaks (opacity, resampling, exaggeration, sky). --- ## 1. DEM source (once) ```js // The DEM tiles you already have – they must be a raster‑dem source map.addSource('terrain-dem', { type: 'raster-dem', url: 'https://my.tileserver.com/terrain/{z}/{x}/{y}.webp', // or a TileJSON URL tileSize: 256, // default, keep it if you’re not sure maxzoom: 12, // whatever your tiles support encoding: 'terrarium' // or 'mapbox' – must match the tiles you serve }); ``` > **Note** – The source is *only* used by elevation‑related layers (`hillshade`, `color‑relief`, `setTerrain`). > Do **not** add a normal `raster` layer that points at this source; that would just show the raw RGB‑encoded DEM. --- ## 2. Hypsometric (color‑relief) layer ```js map.addLayer({ id: 'hypsometric-tint', type: 'color-relief', // <‑‑ the layer type you need source: 'terrain-dem', // the raster‑dem source above paint: { // The colour ramp – an interpolate expression over ["elevation"] 'color-relief-color': [ 'interpolate', ['linear'], // linear interpolation between stops ['elevation'], // special expression that returns metres // ── elevation (m) ── ── colour ─────────────────────── 0, '#2c7bb6', // deep ocean – dark blue 50, '#3b8cc4', // shallow water – lighter blue 200, '#5fa5d0', // near‑shore – cyan‑ish 500, '#abd9e9', // lowland sea‑level – light blue 1000, '#e0f3f8', // low hills – very pale blue 1500, '#ffffbf', // mid‑elevation – yellow‑ish 2500, '#fdae61', // sub‑alpine – orange 3500, '#d73027', // alpine – red‑brown 4500, '#ffffff' // highest peaks – pure white ], // Optional: make the tint semi‑transparent so underlying imagery shows through 'color-relief-opacity': 0.85, // Optional (GL JS ≥ 5.20): control how the DEM is sampled when the map is zoomed out // 'resampling': 'linear' // or 'nearest' – default is 'linear' } }); ``` ### How it works | Piece | What it does | |------|--------------| | `type: 'color-relief'` | Tells MapLibre to treat the source as a DEM and to colour it client‑side. | | `['elevation']` | A **built‑in expression** that returns the elevation (in metres) of the pixel currently being rendered. It can **only** be used inside the `color-relief-color` paint property. | | `interpolate` | Generates a smooth colour gradient between the elevation stops you provide. Use `linear` (default) for a straight‑line ramp; `exponential` is also allowed but rarely needed for hypsometry. | | Stops (`elevation`, `hex colour`) | Define the colour you want at a given height. Add, remove, or adjust them to match the palette you prefer. | | `color-relief-opacity` | Controls how much of the underlying imagery (satellite, vector basemap, etc.) shows through. 1 = opaque, 0 = fully transparent. | | `resampling` (optional) | Determines how DEM values are interpolated when the tile is displayed at a lower resolution. `linear` gives smoother shading; `nearest` is a bit sharper but can look blocky. | --- ## 3. (Optional) Show the terrain in 3‑D and add a sky If you also want a true 3‑D surface you can enable terrain and a sky background. The colour‑relief layer works **both** with a flat map and with 3‑D terrain. ```js // 3‑D terrain (extrudes the DEM) map.setTerrain({ source: 'terrain-dem', exaggeration: 1.2 // tweak to make mountains pop, if you like }); // Pitch the camera so you can see the relief map.easeTo({ pitch: 60, bearing: 0, duration: 1500 }); // Add a sky so the horizon isn’t just the page background map.setSky({ 'sky-color': '#199EF3', 'sky-horizon-blend': 0.5, 'horizon-color': '#ffffff', 'horizon-fog-blend': 0.5, 'fog-color': '#cceeff', 'fog-ground-blend': 0.5 }); ``` > **Important:** The `color‑relief` layer does **not** require `setTerrain()` to work. It will colour the DEM even when the map is flat (pitch = 0). Adding terrain is only for the visual “fly‑over” effect. --- ## 4. Full minimal example (HTML + JS) ```html MapLibre – Hypsometric Tint
``` --- ## 5. Quick checklist | ✅ | Item | |---|------| | **Layer type** | `color-relief` | | **Source** | Same `raster-dem` source you already use | | **Ramp definition** | `color-relief-color` → `interpolate` over `["elevation"]` | | **Opacity** | Set `color-relief-opacity` if you want underlying imagery to show | | **No pre‑rendered tiles** | All coloring happens client‑side | | **Works with 3‑D** | Yes – you can also call `map.setTerrain()` and `map.setSky()` | | **Common pitfalls** | • Using a `raster` layer instead of `color-relief` → you’ll just see the raw DEM image.
• Putting `["elevation"]` outside `color-relief-color` → expression is ignored.
• Forgetting to add the DEM source before the layer → layer will fail to load. | --- ### TL;DR ```json { "id": "hypsometric-tint", "type": "color-relief", "source": "terrain-dem", "paint": { "color-relief-color": [ "interpolate", ["linear"], ["elevation"], 0, "#2c7bb6", 200, "#abd9e9", 1500, "#ffffbf", 2500, "#fdae61", 4000, "#ffffff" ], "color-relief-opacity": 0.8 } } ``` Add that layer after you have a `raster-dem` source, and you’ll get a smooth hypsometric tint (blue → green → brown → white) rendered entirely on the client, with no extra raster tiles required. Happy mapping!

Description: anti-pattern — stacking hillshade layers for multi-directional shading
prompt: My single hillshade layer in MapLibre GL JS looks harsh, how do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Thinking: We need to answer using the skill. Provide explanation of harsh hillshade, use hillshade-method multidir, adjust exaggeration, illumination anchor, colors with alpha, etc. Provide example JSON and maybe code. Also mention not stacking layers. Provide steps.

### Why a Hillshade Can Look “Harsh”

A **hillshade** layer is just a *paint* layer that turns the numeric values in a `raster‑dem` source into light‑and‑shadow.  
If the result is:

* very black shadows / very white highlights  
* “chalky” ridges that dominate the map  
* a flat‑looking surface that only shows the darkest and brightest pixels  

the problem is almost always one (or a combination) of these:

| What it is | Typical cause |
|------------|----------------|
| **Too much contrast** | `hillshade-exaggeration` is too high (default 0.5) or the default `hillshade-method: "standard"` uses a single light direction. |
| **Hard‑edged light** | `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` are opaque (`#000000` / `#FFFFFF`). |
| **Light follows the viewport** | `hillshade-illumination-anchor: "viewport"` makes the light stay at the top of the screen, so when you rotate the map the shadows look “stuck”. |
| **Multiple stacked hillshades** | Adding several hillshade layers with different illumination directions was the old workaround for multi‑directional lighting. It now forces extra draw passes and makes the result even harsher. |

The fix is to **use the newer multi‑directional shading method** (or another softer method) **and tone down the colors**. You can do it in a single layer – no need to stack anything.

---

## 1. Minimal “soft” hillshade configuration

```json
{
  "id": "hillshade",
  "type": "hillshade",
  "source": "terrain-dem",          // your raster‑dem source
  "paint": {
    // 1️⃣ One‑pass, multi‑directional lighting (GL JS 5.5+)
    "hillshade-method": "multidirectional",

    // 2️⃣ Reduce overall contrast
    "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.35,

    // 3️⃣ Make the light follow the map (so shadows rotate with bearing)
    "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map",

    // 4️⃣ Warm, semi‑transparent highlights
    "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.45)",

    // 5️⃣ Cool, semi‑transparent shadows
    "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)"
  }
}
```

### What each line does

| Property | Effect |
|----------|--------|
| **`hillshade-method: "multidirectional"`** | Lights the terrain from several directions in a single pass. This alone softens the harsh black‑and‑white look of the default `standard` method. |
| **`hillshade-exaggeration`** | Scales the intensity of the shading. Values ≈ 0.3‑0.5 give a gentle relief; > 0.6 starts to look “punchy”. |
| **`hillshade-illumination-anchor`** | `"map"` ties the light to the map’s north‑up orientation, so when you rotate the map the shadows rotate too (more natural). Use `"viewport"` only if you deliberately want a fixed‑screen light. |
| **`hillshade-highlight-color` / `hillshade-shadow-color`** | By giving them an **alpha** (the fourth number in `rgba`) you let the underlying imagery show through. Warm highlights (`rgba(255,240,200,…)`) and cool shadows (`rgba(30,40,80,…)`) also improve readability. |
| **No extra layers** | Keep just this one hillshade layer. Stacking several hillshades was the pre‑5.5 hack for multi‑directional lighting; it now just wastes GPU cycles and can make the result even harsher. |

---

## 2. Fine‑tuning tips

| Goal | How to tweak |
|------|--------------|
| **Even softer shadows** | Lower `hillshade-exaggeration` to `0.2‑0.3` or increase the alpha of `hillshade-shadow-color` (e.g. `rgba(30,40,80,0.3)`). |
| **More pronounced ridges** | Raise `hillshade-exaggeration` a little (up to `0.6`) **and** keep the highlight/shadow alphas low (≈ 0.4). |
| **Match a specific light direction** | Keep `hillshade-method: "standard"` (or `"basic"`), then set `hillshade-illumination-direction` (0‑360°) and optionally `hillshade-illumination-anchor: "viewport"` if you want a fixed‑screen sun. |
| **Avoid “flat” look on low‑zoom** | Combine a gentle hillshade with a `color-relief` layer (see the *Color‑relief* skill) – the color‑relief gives a base hypsometric tint while hillshade adds subtle depth. |
| **Performance** | One hillshade layer is cheap. Adding a `color‑relief` layer on top adds a second pass, but still far cheaper than stacking three+ hillshades. |

---

## 3. Full example (including source)

```javascript
// 1️⃣ Add the DEM source (only once)
map.addSource('terrain-dem', {
  type: 'raster-dem',
  url: 'https://tiles.example.com/dem/{z}/{x}/{y}.webp',
  // encoding must match the tiles you serve (terrarium, mapbox, etc.)
  // encoding: 'terrarium'   // optional, defaults to mapbox if omitted
});

// 2️⃣ Add the softened hillshade layer
map.addLayer({
  id: 'hillshade',
  type: 'hillshade',
  source: 'terrain-dem',
  paint: {
    'hillshade-method': 'multidirectional',
    'hillshade-exaggeration': 0.35,
    'hillshade-illumination-anchor': 'map',
    'hillshade-highlight-color': 'rgba(255,240,200,0.45)',
    'hillshade-shadow-color': 'rgba(30,40,80,0.45)'
  }
});
```

That’s it – the map will now show a **smooth, natural‑looking relief** under any raster imagery you have draped on top.

---

## 4. Quick checklist (so you don’t miss anything)

| ✅ | Check |
|----|-------|
| **Only one hillshade layer** (no duplicates) |
| `hillshade-method` set to `"multidirectional"` (or `"basic"`/`"igor"` if you prefer) |
| `hillshade-exaggeration` ≤ 0.5 for a gentle look |
| Highlight & shadow colors use `rgba(..., α)` with α ≈ 0.4‑0.5 |
| `hillshade-illumination-anchor` = `"map"` (unless you need a fixed‑screen sun) |
| No stray `raster-color`, `raster-value`, or Mapbox‑only properties in the layer – they are ignored by MapLibre. |

If you follow the JSON above and the checklist, the harsh black‑and‑white hillshade will be replaced by a **soft, multi‑directional relief** that blends nicely with your base map. Happy mapping!
